lessons.title: Case Study: Reliance and Jio Financial Services, and ITC and ITC Hotels

children.text: Two of India's most widely held stocks demerged a business within eighteen months of each other. Reliance Industries separated its financial services arm into Jio Financial Services in 2023, and ITC separated its hotels business into ITC Hotels in early 2025. Between them, they touched millions of retail demat accounts and almost every Indian equity mutual fund. On the surface they look alike: a giant conglomerate carving out a non-core business. Underneath, they were structured very differently, and those differences decided what shareholders actually received. This lesson runs both through every tool from Chapter 4.

body.text: Two demergers can look identical in the headlines and still hand shareholders very different things. The questions that separate them are always the same: what business moved, at what ratio, how much the parent kept, and what the market had to price on listing day.

children.text: Part 1: Reliance and Jio Financial Services
Why Reliance did it

Reliance's core businesses, oil-to-chemicals, retail and telecom, need huge capital and carry industrial risk. Lending, insurance and asset management are regulated businesses that investors value very differently and that regulators prefer to see ring-fenced from a parent's operating risks. Map it to Lesson 4.1's motives and three stand out: regulatory separation, a different investor base, and the freedom to strike partnerships. In July 2023, the same month the demerger took effect, JFS announced a 50:50 asset management joint venture with BlackRock.
What shareholders received
Because the ratio was 1 for 1 and Reliance kept no stake, every Reliance shareholder became a JFS shareholder in exactly the same proportion. At listing, JFS's shareholding pattern closely
mirrored
Reliance's, promoters included. As Lesson 4.2 showed, the special pre-open session implied ₹261.85 per JFS share.

markDefs.definition: A mirror shareholding means the resulting company starts life with the same shareholders, in the same proportions, as the parent. It happens when all resulting company shares go to parent shareholders pro rata and the parent keeps none.

body.title: Reliance's 19 July 2023 close, split on the record date (₹ per share)
Value what arrived
body.prompt: Neha held 250 Reliance shares on 20 July 2023. Using the implied value of ₹261.85 per JFS share, what was the implied value of the JFS shares she received, in rupees?
body.explanation: At 1 for 1, she received 250 JFS shares. 250 × ₹261.85 = ₹65,462.50. That is the same amount by which her Reliance holding fell in value on the record date: 250 × (₹2,841.85 minus ₹2,580).

children.text: Listing day and the index effect

JFS listed on 21 August 2023 at ₹265 on BSE and hit its 5% lower circuit on its first day, with further lower circuits on the following days. Two forces from Lesson 4.2 were at work. Index funds tracking the Nifty 50 and Sensex had received JFS shares and had to sell once JFS was removed from those indices. And many shareholders who had never chosen to own a financial services start-up simply sold. Neither had anything to do with the long-term worth of the business.

body.text: A 1 for 1 demerger with no stake retained hands the entire new company to shareholders who bought the parent for other reasons. Expect a wave of selling from investors, funds and index trackers who do not want the new business. That selling can create short-term price weakness that has little to do with value.

children.text: The cost split

Reliance announced that 95.32% of shareholders' original cost stays with Reliance and 4.68% moves to JFS, as you worked through in Lesson 4.3. On record date prices, JFS was about 9.2% of the combined market value, roughly double its share of the tax cost.
Part 2: ITC and ITC Hotels
Why ITC did it

ITC's cigarettes and FMCG businesses generate large, steady cash flows with modest capital needs. Hotels are the opposite: capital-intensive, cyclical and slow to earn back investment. For years, investors questioned why cigarette profits funded hotel construction. Separating the hotels business addressed the capital allocation and conglomerate discount motives from Lesson 4.1, while letting ITC Hotels pursue growth through management contracts and partnerships rather than only through owning properties.

children.text: Why the 40% stake changes the maths

Because ITC kept 40%, an ITC shareholder owns the hotels business in two ways: directly through the ITC Hotels shares received, and indirectly through ITC's stake. Your total economic interest in the hotels business does not change. Only the form does.

body.latex: \text{Economic interest in ITC Hotels} = \underbrace{s \times 60\%}_{\text{direct}} + \underbrace{s \times 40\%}_{\text{through ITC}} = s
body.caption: Here s is your percentage ownership of ITC. The split between direct and indirect ownership changes, but the total stays at s.

body.title: Direct stake
body.prompt: A large fund owned 2% of ITC on the record date. What percentage of ITC Hotels did it own directly after receiving its demerger shares?
body.explanation: Shareholders together received 60% of ITC Hotels, pro rata to their ITC holdings. 2% × 60% = 1.2% directly. Through its 2% of ITC, which owns 40% of ITC Hotels, it also holds 2% × 40% = 0.8% indirectly. Total economic interest = 1.2% + 0.8% = 2%, unchanged.

body.title: An odd holding
body.prompt: Vikram held 1,234 ITC shares on 6 January 2025. At 1 ITC Hotels share for every 10 ITC shares, how many whole ITC Hotels shares did he receive?
body.explanation: 1,234 ÷ 10 = 123.4. He received 123 whole ITC Hotels shares. The 0.4 fractional entitlement is handled as the scheme specifies, typically pooled, sold and paid out in cash, as described in Lesson 1.1.

body.title: Why keep 40%?
body.question: Which is the most reasonable explanation for ITC keeping about 40% of ITC Hotels instead of distributing all of it to shareholders, as Reliance did with JFS?
options: To avoid paying tax on the demerger
To give the young listed hotels company a strong anchor shareholder and continued support while it established itself, while still letting shareholders own most of it directly
Because SEBI rules require a parent to keep 40% of every demerged company
To stop ITC Hotels from ever being included in stock market indices
body.explanation: There is no SEBI rule requiring a parent to keep a stake, and the tax treatment does not depend on it. A retained stake signals continued commitment and provides stability for the new company's shareholding. The trade-off is that ITC investors keep indirect exposure to hotels, which partly dilutes the clean separation some wanted.

children.text: Part 3: What the Two Cases Teach

columns.label: Clean break: Reliance and JFS
points: Parent keeps nothing, so the separation is complete
Shareholders get the full value of the new company directly
Mirror shareholding at listing, including the same promoters
More shares change hands after listing as unwilling holders sell
Parent's investors lose all exposure to the carved-out business

columns.label: Anchored separation: ITC and ITC Hotels
points: Parent keeps a large stake, so the separation is partial
Shareholders get most of the new company directly, the rest indirectly
Parent is the new company's largest shareholder
Parent's investors keep indirect exposure to the carved-out business
Parent's results still reflect its share of the new company's performance

cells: Discovered from ITC's special session price
Removal from Nifty 50 and Sensex after listing
Check whether it was retained in or removed from each index

body.title: Describe the JFS shareholding
body.textWithBlank: Because JFS shares were issued 1 for 1 to all Reliance shareholders and Reliance kept none, JFS started life with a ___ shareholding of Reliance's.
body.explanation: A mirror shareholding means the new company's shareholders and their proportions match the parent's at the start. Trading after listing then gradually changes the pattern.

body.title: Tidying up after two demergers
body.scenario: Lata, a retired teacher in Pune, has held Reliance and ITC for over a decade for stability and dividends. After both demergers, her Zerodha account shows four holdings: Reliance, JFS, ITC and ITC Hotels. Her JFS and ITC Hotels positions are each a small fraction of her portfolio. She asks whether she should simply sell the two new stocks.
body.prompt: How should she think about this decision?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Start with fit, not price. She bought for stability and dividends. Ask whether a financial services company building new businesses and a capital-intensive hotels company match that goal. For many income-focused investors, they may not.
2. Remember the ITC difference. Even if she sells ITC Hotels, she keeps indirect hotels exposure through ITC's roughly 40% stake. Selling JFS removes her financial services exposure entirely.
3. Tax first. Both holdings carry her original purchase dates, so gains are long-term. Split her original costs using each company's apportionment announcement before calculating gains, and use the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption on long-term listed equity gains across tax years if the amounts allow.
4. Avoid index-driven timing. Selling in the first days after listing, when index funds and unwilling holders are also selling, can mean selling at a temporarily weak price.
5. Keep it simple. Small positions she does not understand or want can reasonably be sold, but gradually and after checking tax, not as a reaction on listing day.
6. Reinvest with purpose: if she sells, she can add to holdings that match her income goal.

Each company's return on capital and dividend record since listing, to judge whether the separation has improved focus and capital allocation.

body.title: The demerger case study playbook
steps: Identify what business moved and the parent's stated motives
Note the entitlement ratio and whether the parent kept a stake
Record the parent's previous close and special session price, and calculate the implied value per new share
Expect selling after listing from index funds and investors who do not want the new business
Split your cost using the company's apportionment announcement
Decide on each company separately, based on whether it fits your goals

points: Reliance handed all of JFS to its shareholders at 1 for 1, creating a mirror shareholding and a clean break.
ITC kept about 40% of ITC Hotels and gave shareholders about 60% at 1 for 10, so its investors keep indirect hotels exposure.
A retained stake does not change your total economic interest: a 2% ITC holder owns 1.2% of ITC Hotels directly and 0.8% indirectly.
JFS hit lower circuits after listing as index funds and unwilling holders sold, a reminder that post-listing selling can be mechanical.
Each deal answered different motives: regulatory separation and partnerships for Reliance, capital allocation and the conglomerate discount for ITC.
Decide on each new holding by fit with your goals and tax position, not by reacting on listing day.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Figures for Reliance Industries, Jio Financial Services, ITC and ITC Hotels are from public disclosures and news reports and are rounded where noted. Neha, Vikram, Lata and the fund in the examples are fictional. Mentioning a company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
